query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a dense, ultrathin Y2O3 barrier coating onto the surface of a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by limiting oxygen diffusion into the substrate, thereby reducing the formation and spallation of non-protective oxide scales during prolonged exposure in oxidizing environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory HEA that, when untreated, forms mixed and often spalling oxide scales (e.g., CrTaO4-based oxides with dispersed Al2O3/Cr2O3) under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.intervention: Application of a dense, ultrathin Y2O3 coating using physical vapor deposition (PVD).
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 1100°C for up to 200 hours, conditions that mimic extreme-temperature environments for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and well-adhered Y2O3 coating that remains intact at high temperatures, acting as an effective oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The Y2O3 coating, known for its thermal stability and low oxygen permeability, restricts oxygen ingress into the bulk alloy. This barrier reduces the rate of oxidation reactions at the alloy surface, thereby minimizing oxide scale growth and spallation compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Y2O3-coated RHEA is predicted to exhibit a significantly lower weight gain and improved oxide scale integrity during high-temperature exposure compared to the untreated alloy. The coating is expected to reduce the oxidation kinetics by limiting oxygen diffusion, thus enhancing long-term oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated RHEA samples that develop a mixed, sometimes spalling oxide scale with an exponential weight gain (as observed in previous studies, e.g., weight gains around 4-5 mg/cm² at 1100°C over 200 hours).
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the coating may depend on factors such as its uniformity, thickness, and adhesion. If the coating is too thin or poorly bonded, it may spall or degrade under thermal cycling, reducing its protective ability. Additionally, extreme thermal gradients or mechanical stresses may overcome the barrier properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in weight gain and the improvement in scale adherence are uncertain and may require optimization of the coating process. The response might also vary with slight differences in alloy composition and coating microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA samples: one set with an ultrathin Y2O3 coating deposited via PVD and one set left untreated. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation tests in air at 1100°C for 200 hours. Monitor weight gain using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) throughout the exposure period and conduct post-test analyses using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the oxide scale composition, thickness, and adherence.
measurements: TGA for quantifying weight gain during oxidation
XRD for phase identification of the oxide scales
SEM for examining oxide scale morphology and adherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Y2O3-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and improved integrity (e.g., continuous, non-spalled oxide scales) compared to the untreated samples after 200 hours at 1100°C in air.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. decision.trend: Earlier work on NbMoCrTiAl RHEAs introduced ceramic reinforcements (TiC and Al2O3) to boost mechanical strength while retaining some oxidation resistance. More recent studies on WVTaTiCr coatings explored how varying Cr content affects high-temperature oxidation defense by promoting protective surface phases. These efforts highlight the ongoing challenge of achieving a robust, continuous oxide layer capable of sustaining barrier properties at extreme temperatures without compromising the bulk alloy’s mechanical performance.
decision.unsolved: Despite incremental successes, it remains difficult to form and maintain a stable, protective oxide scale on refractory HEAs at very high temperatures. Spallation, scale volatility, and chemical complexity can lead to incomplete surface coverage or mixed oxide formation, limiting long-term oxygen resistance.
decision.lever: Deposit a dense, oxide-based barrier coating (e.g., an ultrathin Al2O3 or Y2O3 layer) on the refractory HEA surface via a high-temperature chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or physical vapor deposition (PVD) process, ensuring strong bonding to mitigate spallation.
decision.why: Building on studies where improved oxidation performance was tied to stable surface oxide layers, a protective coating can act as a dedicated oxygen diffusion barrier. This approach avoids the compositional complexity of adding new elements into the bulk alloy and leverages known protective oxides to address the ongoing gap in long-term oxidation resistance at extreme temperatures.
